problem: Prior differentiable planners (VIN, GPPN) use convolutional structure and propagate value only locally, needing O(D) iterations, so they degrade on large maps and long distances; classical planners need a ground-truth map and re-plan from scratch.
motivation: A learned planner can exploit statistical regularities of maps, is fast at inference (one forward pass), and can be trained end-to-end with a mapper without map supervision. Transformers can attend to any location, so value can propagate between distant points with no obstacles between them, needing roughly O(number of obstacles) iterations rather than O(map size).
key_idea: Use a Transformer with global self-attention over map cells as a differentiable spatial planner (SPT) that propagates distance values over long range, and pre-train and freeze it as the planner in an end-to-end mapper+planner model.
insight: Long-range attention removes the dependence of iteration count on map size: SPT uses a constant N=5 layers, while VIN/GPPN need K=90/60 iterations at M=50 and their accuracy falls. Fig 6 shows the error gap to baselines grows with action distance. Attention maps show heads focusing on obstacles, the goal, and nearby obstacles. Under sparse supervision, map accuracy drops (98.96 to 80.15) but plan accuracy stays high (97.18), since the mapper learns only the minimal map needed for the action distances.
method: Input/Encoder: map m and goal g are stacked as a 2×M×M input and passed through a 2-layer 1×1 conv network, so all obstacle cells share one embedding and all free cells share another; the result is flattened to d×M² tokens.
Transformer: constant sinusoidal positional encoding is added, then N=5 standard Transformer layers (h=8 heads, d=64, FC dim 512) apply global self-attention over all cells.
Decoder: a position-wise linear layer predicts the action distance to the goal at each cell; trained with MSE against Dijkstra distances, with obstacles and unreachable cells set to -1.

End-to-end Mapper+Planner: a Mapper predicts the map from observations, the SPT planner is pre-trained on synthetic maps and frozen, and only action-distance supervision is used to train the mapper (no map labels).

Navigation Mapper: ResNet18 plus FC layers (256, 128, 1) predicts whether the cell in front of each RGB image is an obstacle, taking 4 orientation images per cell and max-pooling the up-to-4 predictions per cell.
Manipulation Mapper: the same SPT architecture with 3×3 conv encoder maps a P×P operational-space image to an M×M configuration-space collision map.
Evaluation setup: a 4-action (N/S/E/W) grid; action accuracy is computed from the minimum-distance neighbour; the baselines' iteration count K is tuned so inference time is at most 1.1× SPT's.

setting.backbone: Spatial Planning Transformer (5-layer Transformer, d=64, 8 heads) as planner; ResNet18-based mapper for navigation, SPT-style Transformer mapper for manipulation (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Synthetic maps: 100K/5K/5K train/val/test per setting (rectangular obstacles for navigation, circular obstacles in configuration space for manipulation); end-to-end navigation uses Gibson scenes via Habitat (72 train/14 val scenes, 36K/7K maps)
setting.observation: Known-map setting: binary obstacle map plus goal map. Unknown-map setting: first-person RGB images 128×128 at 4 orientations per cell (navigation) or a top-down P×P obstacle image (manipulation).
setting.action_space: 4 discrete grid actions (N/S/E/W); a 100-action 10×10 neighbourhood with a low-level controller in the scalability experiment
setting.simulator: Habitat (Gibson scenes) for the navigation experiments; synthetic 2D maps and a 2-DoF planar arm for the rest
setting.privileged: Known-map experiments use the ground-truth obstacle map; the end-to-end experiments use ground-truth action distances (from Dijkstra) as supervision; the Habitat navigation test assumes a perfect partial map from observations so far.

results: SPT reaches 99.41% overall in-distribution planning accuracy vs 92.31% for GPPN, and 95.18% out-of-distribution vs 86.95%. In end-to-end mapping and planning it gets 82.29% plan accuracy vs 63.91% for GPPN, with no map supervision. It is also 1.24–20.22× faster than Dijkstra and A* (runtime table), and reaches 78.0% SR in Habitat vs 47.2% for GPPN.
limitations: Attention over M² tokens has high memory cost, so it scales poorly to large maps (the authors suggest efficient attention or coarser discretization).
Evaluation is limited to small 2D grids with 4 axis-aligned actions, synthetic and Gibson-derived maps, and a 2-DoF arm, with only one small Habitat navigation experiment.
The end-to-end navigation planning accuracy is still modest (66.16%), and the mapper needs 4 orientation images at every cell, which assumes dense observations.
